title: Pitot-Static and Vacuum Systems — How Instruments Work and How They Fail

questions.text: During cruise at 8,000 feet, the pitot tube becomes completely blocked by ice (while the static port remains open and the pitot drain hole also becomes blocked). The pilot begins a climb to 10,000 feet. What does the airspeed indicator show during the climb?

options.label: A
options.text: The ASI is unaffected — ice on the pitot tube exterior does not affect the pressure inside the pitot tube if the aircraft has a pitot heat system; the blocked tube only affects the ASI when pitot heat is OFF

options.label: B
options.text: The ASI freezes at the airspeed reading at the moment of blockage, then slowly returns to zero — the frozen pitot pressure bleeds away through micro-gaps in the pitot system seals; as the pressure equalizes to static, the ASI reads zero within 5-8 minutes of the blockage

options.label: C
options.text: The ASI INCREASES (over-reads) during the climb — with the pitot tube blocked and drain hole also blocked, the ram pressure in the pitot line is FROZEN at the value it held when the ice sealed the tube; as the aircraft climbs to 10,000 feet, static pressure decreases; the ASI measures the DIFFERENCE between frozen pitot pressure and decreasing static pressure; this difference increases as static drops, causing the ASI to erroneously show an increasing (higher than actual) airspeed

options.label: D
options.text: The ASI drops to zero — a completely blocked pitot tube means no ram pressure enters the ASI; with no impact pressure, the instrument reads the minimum value; the static port being open is irrelevant to airspeed reading since airspeed requires pitot input

questions.explanation: This question tests the multi-step inference that most students find counter-intuitive. The ASI measures: pitot pressure MINUS static pressure = dynamic pressure (airspeed). With pitot tube blocked AND drain hole blocked: the pitot line is hermetically sealed. The pressure inside the pitot line is frozen at the value when ice blocked the tube (let's call it P_pitot = constant). As the aircraft climbs to 10,000 feet: static pressure DECREASES (altitude increases → pressure decreases). The ASI now measures: P_pitot (CONSTANT) - P_static (DECREASING). The difference INCREASES. The ASI reads progressively higher than actual airspeed — in a climb with blocked pitot, the instrument reads increasing airspeed. This is dangerous: the pilot may think they are overspeeding and reduce power, actually decelerating toward stall. If the drain hole were OPEN (not blocked): static pressure would bleed into the pitot line through the drain hole, equalizing the pitot side → ASI reads near zero. This is the distinction between a pitot-with-open-drain blockage (ASI → zero) and pitot-with-closed-drain blockage (ASI → over-reads in climb, under-reads in descent).

questions.text: During descent from 12,000 feet, the pilot suspects the static port has become blocked. Altimeter reads 12,000 feet. VSI shows zero. Airspeed indicator appears to show the aircraft is slower than expected for the descent configuration. What confirms static blockage?

options.label: A
options.text: The VSI reading zero alone is enough to confirm static blockage — the VSI is the most sensitive static instrument and will show the blockage first; the altimeter and ASI may take longer to reflect the blockage

options.label: B
options.text: None of the described symptoms confirm static blockage — all three instruments showing these readings could also be caused by the aircraft actually maintaining 12,000 feet in level flight with a slight power reduction reducing airspeed; the pilot should compare with GPS altitude to confirm whether the aircraft is actually descending

options.label: C
options.text: The altimeter reading 12,000 while descending confirms the static port is blocked — because if static were open, the altimeter would be decreasing as the aircraft descends; a frozen altimeter reading in descent is the definitive sign of static blockage

options.label: D
options.text: All three indicators together confirm it: (1) altimeter FROZEN at 12,000 feet (not decreasing in descent = static not sensing increasing pressure below the freeze point), (2) VSI reading ZERO despite an active descent (not sensing pressure change rate), (3) ASI reading LOWER than expected (pitot is sensing increasing ram pressure in descent as speed increases, but static is stuck at 12,000 ft pressure; the differential is smaller than actual → underreads); together these confirm static port blockage

questions.explanation: A blocked static port produces a characteristic 3-instrument signature that distinguishes it from situational interpretation: (1) ALTIMETER FROZEN: with static blocked, the altimeter reference pressure (static) does not change even as the aircraft descends into higher-pressure air; the altimeter reads the pressure altitude at which the port became blocked. (2) VSI READS ZERO: the VSI measures RATE OF CHANGE of static pressure through its calibrated leak; with static pressure frozen, there is no change → VSI reads zero regardless of actual vertical movement. (3) ASI UNDERREADS (in descent): pitot pressure increases in descent (airspeed increases for most descents); static is frozen at 12,000 ft pressure level; the differential (pitot measured - static frozen) is smaller than actual because real static should be higher (lower altitude = higher pressure), but it's stuck at the 12,000 ft value → apparent airspeed is less than actual. All three instruments showing the described pattern simultaneously is the definitive confirmation. The correct action: activate ALTERNATE STATIC source and note the transition (altimeter briefly jumps, then settles slightly high; VSI briefly shows activity). The combination test is the full diagnostic approach.

questions.text: An IFR pilot is on final approach using the alternate static source after the primary port became blocked during an earlier descent. The altimeter shows an altitude that appears to indicate the aircraft is at the Published Decision Altitude (DA) for the ILS approach. The runway environment is not visible. The pilot continues 50 feet below the published DA because 'the runway must be close.' What is the specific hazard created by alternate static use that the pilot overlooked?

options.label: A
options.text: The altimeter OVER-READS when on alternate static in an unpressurized aircraft — cabin pressure is slightly lower than outside static pressure; when alternate static is selected, the altimeter reference is this slightly lower cabin pressure; lower pressure = instrument reads HIGHER altitude than actual; if the pilot sees the altimeter at the published DA of (e.g.) 800 feet, the actual altitude is slightly BELOW 800 feet; the DA reached on alternate static was crossed earlier than the instrument indicated

options.label: B
options.text: No specific hazard — alternate static is an FAA-certified backup system; instruments on alternate static are equally accurate as on primary static; the pilot's decision to continue below DA is the primary error, unrelated to the alternate static selection

options.label: C
options.text: The alternate static source causes the altimeter to UNDER-READ — cabin pressure is higher than outside static air; with higher cabin pressure as the reference, the altimeter thinks it is at a lower-pressure altitude than it actually is; the instrument reads lower than actual altitude; the pilot at the apparent DA is actually higher than DA

options.label: D
options.text: The flight below DA is the only error — alternate static does not introduce directional altitude errors; it introduces a random ±10 foot error from vibration entering the static reference through the cabin venting; this error is non-systematic and does not affect the direction of the altitude reading

questions.explanation: This is a precision instrument approach hazard. In unpressurized aircraft with an interior alternate static source: cabin pressure is slightly LOWER than ambient static pressure. Why? Ram air through the cockpit ventilation system creates a slight positive pressure relative to the outside static, or ventilation creates a slight suction — depending on design. Most POHs note that alternate static results in the altimeter reading HIGHER (approximately 50 feet for some aircraft). The flight implications are significant: if the published DA is 800 feet MSL and the altimeter (with alternate static) reads 800 feet, the actual altitude is approximately 750 feet MSL — already below the DA. The pilot continuing '50 feet below the apparent DA' is actually flying approximately 100+ feet below the published DA. This can place the aircraft in contact with obstructions during the approach phase. POHs document the alternate static correction factor for this reason — pilots must add the correction to determine actual altitude. The approach briefing for alternate static flights should include: 'Note: altimeter reads [correction] feet high on alternate static — actual decision altitude is [corrected reading].'

questions.text: On a night IFR flight in IMC, the vacuum pump fails. The pilot checks the suction gauge and confirms it reads zero. Which of the following instrument configurations describes 'partial panel' — the instruments that remain reliable?

options.label: A
options.text: Attitude indicator, turn coordinator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, and magnetic compass — only the heading indicator fails; the attitude indicator continues to function on residual gyro spin for approximately 30 minutes after vacuum failure

options.label: B
options.text: Turn coordinator (TC), altimeter, airspeed indicator, and magnetic compass — the TC is electrically powered and survives vacuum failure; the AI and HI are vacuum gyros and are now unreliable; attitude must be inferred from TC (wings level/rate of turn indicator) + altimeter trend + ASI; the compass provides heading with awareness of turning and acceleration errors

options.label: C
options.text: Attitude indicator and heading indicator, with backup from the turn coordinator — vacuum gyros maintain reliable indication for 10-15 minutes after vacuum loss; the TC is the final backup after complete gyro rundown; the 10-15 minute window allows the pilot to navigate to VMC conditions

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above — total vacuum failure in IMC is an immediate non-survivable emergency in single-engine aircraft; no partial-panel flying is feasible at night in IMC; the pilot must immediately declare an emergency and request a radar-guided descent

questions.explanation: Partial panel configuration after vacuum failure consists of the ELECTRICALLY POWERED and MECHANICAL instruments: (1) TURN COORDINATOR (TC): electrically powered gyroscope — specifically designed to remain operational when vacuum fails. Provides: bank angle indication (not precise pitch but confirms wings level vs. banked), rate-of-turn indication (standard rate = 3°/sec, useful for timed turns to headings). (2) ALTIMETER: static instrument — no power source required. Remains fully functional after vacuum or electrical failure. Provides altitude and, by trend monitoring, vertical speed. (3) AIRSPEED INDICATOR: pitot-static — no power. Remains functional. Provides airspeed and, when combined with altitude trend, can confirm pitch. (4) MAGNETIC COMPASS: purely mechanical — no power. Provides heading with known error corrections (ANDS, OSSC). The 'attitude indicator survives' answer incorrectly includes the AI as surviving — the AI IS a vacuum gyro and FAILS at vacuum loss (though it may continue temporarily on residual spin). The critical judgment: do NOT trust the AI or HI after vacuum failure confirmation. They may appear to read correctly for several more minutes and then give false indications — the partial panel pilot MUST explicitly disregard them and cover them to avoid unconscious cross-check. The 'AI and HI remain reliable' answer's 10-15 minute residual window may be dangerously optimistic — actual rundown depends on gyro quality and load.

questions.text: In cruise at 7,500 feet VMC, the suction gauge shows 1.8 in. Hg (normal: 4.5-5.5 in. Hg). The attitude indicator and heading indicator appear to be functioning normally. What is the correct immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Check if the suction regulator valve needs adjustment — the 1.8 in. Hg reading indicates the regulator may have drifted below the set point; the pilot can adjust the suction regulator from the cockpit on most aircraft equipped with adjustable vacuum systems

options.label: B
options.text: The instruments are functioning normally, indicating the suction gauge is faulty — when the gyro instruments are reliable, the suction gauge may be malfunctioning; continue flight normally and report the suction gauge for maintenance on landing

options.label: C
options.text: Treat this as a vacuum system failure — at 1.8 in. Hg, the vacuum pump is producing insufficient suction to maintain gyro spin; the AI and HI may appear normal for a few more minutes because the gyros are still spinning on residual momentum; they WILL degrade and become unreliable; begin transition to partial panel immediately; cover the AI and HI to avoid unconscious cross-checking of deteriorating instruments; navigate by TC, altimeter, ASI, and compass; continue VFR to the nearest airport

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce altitude to 3,000 feet — at lower altitudes, atmospheric density increases provide better vacuum pump performance; the suction gauge will recover to normal range with the increased air density available to the vacuum pump

questions.explanation: At 1.8 in. Hg suction (vs. normal 4.5-5.5 in. Hg), the vacuum pump has failed or significantly degraded. The deceptive aspect of this scenario is the one that kills IFR pilots: the AI and HI still APPEAR normal. This is because gyroscopes maintain their orientation by angular momentum — once spinning at 10,000-15,000 RPM, they can maintain near-reliable indication for 3-10 minutes after suction is lost, gradually decelerating and starting to precess or tumble. The pilot who trusts the AI and HI while the vacuum is at 1.8 in. Hg is flying on instruments that are degrading in real time with no reliable indicator of when they cross from 'slightly off' to 'completely wrong.' The correct discipline: LOW SUCTION = VACUUM FAILURE. Treat it as total vacuum failure regardless of apparent AI/HI reliability. COVER the AI and HI immediately to prevent unconscious cross-checking of deteriorating data. Transition deliberately and explicitly to partial panel instruments (TC, altimeter, ASI, compass). In VMC: continue VFR to the nearest airport maintaining VFR for the remainder of flight. The 'attribute it to gauge failure' answer (attribute to gauge failure) represents the most common fatal error — when two systems conflict, particularly when one is a vacuum gauge and the other is a gyro instrument biased by the same malfunctioning vacuum source, trust the gauges over the 'feel' of the instruments.

questions.text: A pilot flying in the mid-latitudes of the northern hemisphere is on a heading of 090° (east) and accelerates rapidly from 80 to 100 knots on a straight-and-level path. What does the magnetic compass temporarily indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: The compass rotates continuously during acceleration — acceleration on any heading causes the pendulous vanes to temporarily lose contact with the compass card; the instrument rotates freely for 3-5 seconds before re-engaging the magnetic field and returning to the correct heading

options.label: B
options.text: The compass temporarily indicates a heading SOUTH of 090° — acceleration on an east heading causes the compass card to swing southward, showing a heading greater than 090° (e.g., 120-135°)

options.label: C
options.text: The compass is unaffected by acceleration on an east heading — ANDS errors only apply to north/south headings; on an east or west heading, the compass reads accurately during acceleration

options.label: D
options.text: The compass dips toward magnetic north and temporarily shows a heading northward of 090° — ANDS mnemonic: Accelerate North; on a east heading, rapid acceleration causes the compass pendulous vanes to swing, temporarily displaying a northerly (lower-number heading) error

questions.explanation: The ANDS mnemonic describes compass acceleration errors in the northern hemisphere: A = Accelerate → N = North error. D = Decelerate → S = South error. On a heading of 090° (east), during acceleration: the magnetic dip component causes the compass float to swing toward magnetic north (lower heading numbers). The pilot sees the compass temporarily reading a heading North-of-090 (e.g., 060-070°) before returning to 090° as the acceleration ceases. This means: on an east heading with rapid acceleration, the compass MISLEADS that the aircraft has turned slightly NORTH (the compass shows a lower heading number). The reverse: on a 090° heading with deceleration, the compass shows an apparent southward turn (higher heading number). ANDS is most pronounced on east/west headings because the north-south magnetic dip component is perpendicular to the direction of acceleration, maximizing the pendulous vane response. On north or south headings, the ANDS error is minimal or negligible (the dip component is aligned with the direction of flight). The 'compass is unaffected' answer inverts the correct answer — ANDS errors are MOST pronounced on east/west headings, not absent.

questions.text: A student pilot is practicing partial panel under the hood. The vacuum system shows normal, but the instructor has covered the AI and HI for the exercise. The student is in a left standard-rate turn to roll out on a magnetic heading of 180° (south). Approaching 180° on the TC, the student hesitates, then continues the turn 15° past because 'it didn't feel like I was at south on the compass.' What is the error pattern and correct technique?

options.label: A
options.text: The student made a ROLLOUT error — turns through south require the pilot to OVERSHOOT (continue past the target heading) because the magnetic compass LEADS actual heading when turning through south (compass shows south before the aircraft is actually heading south); to stop AT 180°, the pilot should stop the turn BEFORE 180° appears on the compass — roll out approximately 10-15° early; continuing 15° PAST 180° means the aircraft is at approximately 195° heading, overshot to a southsouthwesterly heading

options.label: B
options.text: The turning error to south is unpredictable — the amount of lead or lag varies with bank angle, airspeed, and latitude; the student should reference the turn coordinator ONLY for rollout timing and disregard the magnetic compass entirely during the turn

options.label: C
options.text: The student correctly continued past 180° — turns to south are slow to register on the magnetic compass due to the ANDS effect; the extra 15° is a reasonable compensation for compass lag when rolling out on a southerly heading

options.label: D
options.text: The student made the correct compensation — when turning to south, the pilot must overshoot because the compass lags; rolling out 15° past the compass reading of 180° corrects for the lag and results in an actual 180° heading

questions.explanation: The OSSC mnemonic for turning errors: Overshoot South, (Undershoot North). When turning TO south: the compass LEADS (shows south before the aircraft is actually heading south). Correct technique: roll out EARLY — before the compass shows 180°, the aircraft is already AT 180°. If the pilot waits until the compass shows 180° to roll out, the actual heading has passed 180° and is continuing to turn. Degree of lead: approximately 10-20° depending on latitude (higher latitudes = more dip = more error). The student in this scenario: saw 180° on the compass and then CONTINUED 15° past — resulting in an actual heading of approximately 195°. To correct: start the rollout at approximately 165-170° on the compass when turning to 180° (south). Then confirm with the final steady compass reading after wings level. Conversely, when turning to NORTH: compass LAGS. Roll out LATE — continue the turn past where you think north should be until the compass shows north approaching, then stop. The student's instinct ('didn't feel at south') is the spatial disorientation / vestibular illusion trap — 'feel' is unreliable in the cockpit. Trust instruments. The compass for turning through south: OVERSHOOT means the COMPASS overshoots, so the PILOT must stop EARLY to match it.
questions.sjt_rationale: The student's reliance on 'feel' instead of instrument reading, combined with a misunderstanding of the compass turning error direction, compounds into a significant heading error. Partial panel requires disciplined adherence to the OSSC principle — not improvised corrections based on vestibular sense.

questions.text: A pilot intends to file IFR and depart into IMC conditions with visible moisture and temperatures near freezing at altitude. The pitot heat system is inoperative (confirmed by the A&P as non-functional). The pilot argues: 'The alternate static is available so the static side is backed up — I can fly IFR without pitot heat.' Is this a legally and operationally sound argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The decision depends on the MEL — if the aircraft has an approved MEL that permits dispatch with pitot heat inoperative, the pilot may legally dispatch; most Part 91 light aircraft do not have MELs, meaning any required equipment that is inoperative grounds the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.7

options.label: B
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.205(d)(3) lists pitot heat as required equipment for IFR operations when the aircraft is certified for IFR and equipped with pitot heat; operating with an inoperative pitot heat system in IMC with icing conditions subjects the ASI to icing failure; without ASI (the only airspeed instrument), the pilot cannot safely manage airspeed, stall margin, or performance; the aircraft may not be dispatched IFR with piots heat inoperative under these conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the pilot may use the GPS groundspeed as the primary airspeed reference in IMC if pitot heat is inoperative; GPS groundspeed provides an accurate airspeed substitute for IFR navigation when wind is known; the FAA has approved this as an alternative means of compliance for pitot heat inoperative operations

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the alternate static source satisfies the static port requirement; pitot heat affects only the pitot tube and therefore only the ASI; IFR flight with a known-inoperative pitot heat system is permitted if the alternate static provides adequate backup for the altimeter and VSI

questions.explanation: The pilot's argument conflates two separate systems. Alternate static addresses the STATIC PORT (which feeds the altimeter, VSI, and static side of the ASI). Pitot heat addresses the PITOT TUBE (which feeds the pitot-impact side of the ASI ONLY). They are physically separate parts of two different subsystems. With icing conditions and inoperative pitot heat: the pitot tube can accumulate ice, blocking the ram pressure input to the ASI. Result: the ASI fails (reads zero or erroneous). The altimeter and VSI (static-only) remain functional, but the ASI is the ONLY airspeed indicator. Without airspeed: the pilot cannot identify stall approach, cannot manage airspeed for approaches and departure, cannot maintain Vy or Vx for performance. This is a critical instruments failure that is unacceptable for IFR IMC operations. Per 14 CFR 91.205(d), for IFR operations in aircraft certificated with pitot heat: pitot heat is a required IFR instrument. An inoperative pitot heat system in icing conditions makes the aircraft unairworthy for the intended IFR icing-potential flight. The 'GPS groundspeed substitute' answer invents GPS groundspeed as an ASI substitute — GPS groundspeed includes wind component and does not indicate true airspeed relative to the air mass, which is what determines stall speed.
